summary: Changes the IETF standards process in RFC 2026, cutting the standards track from three maturity levels to two. It is a Best Current Practice. The aim is to make advancing a specification simpler and to reflect how the process was already working in practice.

eli5.summary: Imagine a video game with three levels where almost nobody played the middle one. The rule-makers removed it, so now there are just two levels to climb.

questions: how many standards track maturity levels
how the ietf standards process changed
what are the criteria for internet standard
what does rfc 6410 change in rfc 2026
subtitle: The IETF standards track goes from three maturity levels to two, and annual review is dropped.

tldr.problem: Documents had trouble advancing through Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Standard, and most stayed at Proposed Standard. Very few advanced in the last decade.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6410 merges Draft Standard and Standard into one level, Internet Standard. Advancement is judged by widespread deployment of independent implementations, and the annual review is dropped.
tldr.outcome: The standards track has two levels, Proposed Standard and Internet Standard. This BCP updates RFC 2026.

today: RFC 6410 is a Best Current Practice and updates RFC 2026. No later RFC is listed as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why Change the Ladder
sections.content:
RFC 2026 defined three maturity levels: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Standard. The authors note that the vast majority of Standards Track documents are published as Proposed Standards and never advance. Very few specifications advanced in the last decade.

The IESG discussed many proposals in May 2010, and a plenary at IETF 78 in July 2010 showed significant support for two tiers. The stated goal is an environment where lessons from implementation and deployment are used to improve specifications, including removing complexity from unused features.
sections.eli5: Almost everyone stopped on the first step of a three-step staircase. So the builders removed a step to make the climb more sensible.

sections.title: The Two Maturity Levels
sections.content:
The Standards Track now has Proposed Standard and Internet Standard. The requirements for Proposed Standard stay exactly as in RFC 2026, with nothing added and nothing relaxed. Internet Standard merges Draft Standard and Standard. The new name avoids confusion between "Draft Standard" and "Internet-Draft".

Previously, RFC 2026 asked for an interoperability report as an interim step before widespread deployment. This document asks to measure interoperability through widespread deployment of multiple implementations from different code bases, which combines the two metrics into one. A specification is likely to be revised as it advances, and the IESG judges how significant the changes are. A significant revision may need more time at Proposed Standard.
sections.eli5: There is now a starter level and a finished level. To get to the finished level, lots of people must already be using it happily.

sections.title: Advancing to Internet Standard
sections.content:
The IESG holds an IETF-wide Last Call of at least four weeks on the request for reclassification, which comes with an explanation of how the criteria are met. If there is consensus, the RFC is reclassified without publishing a new RFC. The criteria are:

  1. At least two independent interoperating implementations with widespread deployment and successful operational experience.
  2. No errata that would make a new implementation fail to interoperate with deployed ones.
  3. No unused features that greatly increase implementation complexity.
  4. If patented or controlled technology is required, at least two independent, separate and successful uses of the licensing process.
sections.eli5: To win the top badge, at least two different teams must have built it, used it widely, found no bad bugs, and not made it needlessly complicated.

sections.title: Transition and Removed Requirements
sections.content:
Anything at Proposed Standard stays there. Anything at Standard is immediately reclassified as Internet Standard. Documents at the abandoned Draft Standard level keep that classification unless something happens. A Draft Standard can become an Internet Standard as soon as the criteria are met, or, any time after two years from approval of this BCP, the IESG may reclassify it as Proposed Standard.

Two requirements are removed. The annual review of Proposed and Draft Standards, which RFC 2026 called for, had not taken place in practice and its absence revealed no ill effects, so no review cycle is imposed at any level. A formal interoperability report is also no longer required, because deployment and use are sufficient to show interoperability. RFC 5657 can still help with interoperability testing.
sections.eli5: Everyone already on the first step stays put, and everyone on the top step stays on top. The skipped middle step is cleaned up over time, and the yearly check-up nobody did is cancelled.

sections.title: Earlier Proposals and Security
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a two-tier Standards Track has been proposed many times. It names proposals from 2003 (Spencer Dawkins, Charlie Perkins and Dave Crocker), 2004 (Scott Bradner), June 2005 (Brian Carpenter) and 2006 (Ran Atkinson). It also draws on the May 2010 IESG discussion, the IETF 78 plenary in July 2010 and a November 2010 proposal.

On security, the RFC says only that it does not directly affect the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: Lots of people had suggested this idea over the years. This time enough people agreed, and it is only a rule change, so it does not make anything less safe.
